title: Circular DNA exposes a weakness in cancer cells
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02966-8

Repetitive sequences make extrachromosomal DNA vulnerable to breaks, which could be exploited for therapy — but might also promote tumour evolution.
headline: Cancer cells' extra DNA loops have a hidden weakness researchers can exploit.
why_it_matters: Cancer cells often carry extra circular DNA (DNA loops floating outside the main chromosomes) that help them survive and resist drugs. If scientists can make these circles break apart, it could stop tumors from growing or becoming resistant to treatment — potentially opening new ways to fight cancer.
key_findings: Cancer cells accumulate circular DNA (small loops of genetic material that exist separately from the main chromosome bundles), which act like a survival advantage for the tumor.
These circular DNA pieces contain repeated sequences (sections of genetic code copied many times, like a stuttering phrase in a sentence), making them fragile and prone to breaking.
The repeated sequences are a weakness because they make the circular DNA unstable — it breaks more easily than normal DNA would.
This vulnerability could be exploited therapeutically — researchers might be able to deliberately damage these circles to weaken cancer cells.
However, breaking this circular DNA might paradoxically help some cancer cells evolve and adapt, so the approach could be a double-edged sword.
methods_snapshot: Researchers analyzed the structure and stability of extrachromosomal DNA (genetic material floating outside the main chromosome) from cancer cells, examining how repetitive sequences make it vulnerable to breaks. They used computational and molecular analysis to understand what makes these circles fragile and how cells might repair or fail to repair the damage.

glossary.definition: Genetic material that exists as separate loops or circles outside the main chromosome bundles in a cell.
Sections of DNA code that repeat multiple times in the same location, like a musical phrase repeated over and over.
DNA shaped like a closed loop rather than a straight line, similar to the difference between a circle and a line drawn on paper.
A package of DNA containing thousands of genes; humans normally have 46 of them bundled in the cell nucleus.
The process by which cancer cells accumulate new mutations and adaptations over time, often making them harder to treat.

cancer_types: Multiple cancer types studied (specific types not detailed in abstract)
limitations: The abstract does not specify which cancer types were studied or how broadly these findings apply across different tumors. Additionally, while the weakness is identified, the paper acknowledges that exploiting it therapeutically could backfire by accelerating tumor evolution — meaning this knowledge alone does not immediately translate to safe clinical treatments.
